source.title: More data or more parameters? Investigating the effect of data structure on generalization
source.authors: Stéphane d'Ascoli; Marylou Gabrié; Levent Sagun; G. Biroli

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures double-descent behavior in random-feature models and reports that the peak depends on loss, data structure, and noise; in particular, it is absent or attenuated for logistic loss where it appears for square loss.
record.gate_note: The paper varies the number of random features P and, in appendix phase-space plots, the number of samples N. It also reports training-loss curves and test-error outcomes on MNIST and CIFAR10. The order parameters Q and M are not rows because they do not themselves measure the test-error curve in the claim. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives replica-exact train and test error curves for random-feature classifiers on structured (strong/weak features) data and checks them numerically and on MNIST/CIFAR10. It shows double descent in P at P=N for square loss, a peak that is absent or strongly attenuated for logistic loss, and (N,P) phase spaces with sample-wise peaks. This is a new setting (anisotropic data, classification, any convex loss) with direct results on V3, V4 and V6. T5 is defensible because of the logistic-loss result, but the paper does not argue against the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that loss function and data structure jointly shape the generalization curve of random-feature models. Square loss shows a double-descent peak at P=N, while logistic loss removes or strongly reduces it, which they attribute to implicit regularization. Logistic loss also generalizes better on easy, aligned tasks, and the gap widens as the task gets easier. They note these lazy-regime results may not carry over to deep networks with feature learning.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes random-feature models with a fixed random first layer and trained second-layer weights, using replica calculations and numerical experiments; it is not a reproduction of deep-network size, epoch, or sample sweeps from the cited original work.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on loss function, label-flip probability, data anisotropy and teacher-data alignment; the study also varies activation function and regularization in appendix experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: For logistic loss, the effective interpolation threshold (where train loss plateaus near zero) shifts with data structure: lower when aligned, higher when misaligned, and up with label noise. For square loss it stays at P=N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The location of the interpolation threshold depends on data structure and loss, not only on parameter count versus sample count.

fits_no_version.finding: Order parameter Q peaks at the interpolation threshold for square loss. For logistic loss, Q grows as a power law with P, which the authors say shields the peak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-norm growth under logistic loss acts as implicit regularization that removes the double-descent peak.

record.problems: The main model is a random-feature/lazy-learning model rather than a trained deep network. Several outcomes are qualitative descriptions of figures rather than tabulated values. Numerical experiments in Fig. 2 report standard deviations over 10 runs, but the plotted values are not stated in text.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the tested versions were omitted.

untested.parts: Only random-feature (lazy, second-layer-trained) models are studied; there are no trained deep networks.
No fixed-P numeric sequence showing test error rising with N; the evidence is phase-space heatmaps only.
Only random-feature models are tested; the transition from a classical U-shape is not examined across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested. The logistic effective threshold shifts with data structure, but this is not framed as a predictor of the peak.
Optimally tuned regularization is not tested; λ is fixed at 1e-3 or 0.1.

missing.what: Isotropic square-loss phase space: double-descent peak 'clearly visible at N=P', which is sample-wise evidence for V3 beyond the anisotropic row R13.
Logistic noiseless peak at N>P that shifts to N=P with label noise (Δ=0.4).
Fig. 9: as saliency rx rises from 1 to 1000, an overfitting peak at N=D forms (rx=10, 100) and then vanishes. Evidence that a second peak depends on data anisotropy.

record.verdict_notes: The theory is replica-based, non-rigorous but matched by simulations at D=100. The interpolation point is P=N, which equals P=D here because N/D=1. The appendix uses ReLU and λ=0.1, while the main text uses Tanh and λ=1e-3. Most evidence is from figures with no tabulated values. Labelling noiseless logistic as limits_scope rather than challenges for V4 is a judgment call: the peak is absent, but risk still improves past the interpolation point.

versions.untested_parts: The model-wise results are for random-feature models, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The sample-wise evidence is reported as phase-space behavior and an overfitting region around N=D; no tabulated fixed-P numerical sequence is given.
The study tests random-feature models, not a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study compares noiseless and label-flipped conditions and different losses at stated regularization settings. It does not test multiple/triple descent or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether this turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
